title: Chunked Delivery vs Multiplexed Frames — field notes
content:
Context:
These are working notes from a small exploratory effort to measure the end-to-end cost of two common streaming strategies we use in the runtime: (A) application-level chunked delivery (emit small chunks as tokens are produced) and (B) relying on HTTP/2 / gRPC multiplexed frame aggregation (larger frames, fewer syscalls). We want to understand the latency tail behavior, CPU/spawn overhead, and how intermediaries (proxies like Envoy) and network stacks amplify or attenuate the tradeoffs.

Motivation / Question set:
- For low-latency generation workloads (short responses, interactive chat), is sending small incremental chunks better than coalescing into fewer, larger frames?
- How do proxies (Envoy) and HTTP/2 flow control/windowing interact with small writes?
- What are the dominant sources of extra latency (syscalls, TLS record boundaries, proxy buffering, congestion control)?
- Can we tune OS/TCP/HTTP2 settings or runtime write strategy to get the best of both worlds (low tail latency with reasonable CPU)?

Testbed overview (mini lab):
- Server: 8 vCPU, 2 x A100-ish type GPUs (model runner separate process), Linux 5.15, OpenSSL 3.0, runtime under test: local branch chunking-experiments (see PR).
- Client: colocated VM, synthetic load generator (custom python async client), ghz for gRPC, wrk2 for HTTP/1.1 variants.
- Proxy: Envoy sidecar (v1.30) in front of server for proxy experiments.
- Network: small-instances same AZ to minimize cross-region variability; we still exercise RTT artificially with tc (10ms/20ms emulation).
- Observability: tcpdump (pcap), perf for CPU hotspots, eBPF (bcc) to measure syscall counts and bytes-per-write, OpenSSL s_time and ss for socket states, strace for write patterns on a subset of runs.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 (manual frame control as allowed by netty/grpc), gRPC streaming (grpc-java and grpc-go variants), HTTP/2 with explicit MAX_FRAME_SIZE tweaks.
- Chunk sizes: 64B, 256B, 1KB, 8KB, coalesced (>= 32KB).
- Server batching policy: immediate (emit token as ready), micro-batch (accumulate up to N tokens or t ms), coalesce-on-rt (adaptive pacing).
- Network conditions: baseline (nominal AZ), RTT=10ms, RTT=25ms, small bandwidth limit 5 Mbps to force backpressure.
- Proxy on/off and Envoy buffer/flush settings.

Key measurements collected:
- Latency p50/p95/p99 for first-byte (time until client receives first chunk) and full-response completion
- Per-request server CPU cycles and per-token syscall count (write/syscall patterns)
- TLS records emitted and their sizes
- Envoy queueing time (measured via headers added by a small filter)
- Retransmissions / TCP-level stalls observed in tcpdump

Representative results (summarized observations, numbers are medians from N=2000 requests per configuration unless noted):
1) Small chunks (64–256B) with application-level immediate emitting:
   - First-byte p50: ~10–12ms (baseline RTT=10ms), p95: ~35–60ms, p99: 120–220ms
   - CPU: ~15–25% higher CPU per request due to syscall overhead and TLS record sealing overhead
   - Syscalls: average 12 write/sendfile calls per 1KB sent (many small writes); TLS produced many small records (~record size ~1–2KB depending on implementation)
   - Proxy: when Envoy is present with default buffering, observed extra 5–40ms queueing at p95 depending on its flush thresholds; some small writes were coalesced by Envoy into larger frames which helped throughput but increased p95 for first bytes

2) Multiplexed/coalesced frames (server waits to emit 1–8KB frames):
   - First-byte p50: slightly higher (~12–15ms) because server holds to coalesce, p95: much lower (~25–35ms) since fewer indeterminate small writes reduce queuing variability
   - CPU: lower per-request CPU, fewer syscalls, fewer TLS record seals
   - Proxy: cooperative — Envoy sees fewer frames and lower internal queuing; p99 improved vs naive small-chunk strategy

3) HTTP/2 tuning (SETTINGS MAX_FRAME_SIZE and initial window tweaks):
   - Increasing MAX_FRAME_SIZE to 32KB and raising initial window size reduced stalls for coalesced frames and improved throughput without increasing first-byte p50 significantly
   - However, on networks with small RTTs but headroom, larger frames increase serialization time when packets are lost (more data to retransmit) — tradeoff exists

4) Backpressure and bandwidth-limited scenarios (5 Mbps)
   - Frequent small writes caused long tail due to buffer bloat: server continued to push small TLS records which filled kernel queues -> higher queuing delay before bytes hit wire
   - Coalescing reduced queue churn and smoothed out bursts; adaptive pacing (emit small chunks but only when socket writable/low buffer) had best tail behavior

Profile notes (root causes identified):
- Syscall and TLS sealing: small writes map to many write/send calls; each call triggers a TLS seal operation that is nontrivial (AES-GCM encryption and HMAC). This is the dominant CPU cost for ultra-low token sizes.
- Epoll wakeups/context-switches: many small writes caused frequent wakeups. The epoll->worker interactions showed increased context switches at high concurrency leading to jitter in p95/p99.
- Proxy coalescing behavior: many proxies buffer small writes to assemble larger downstream frames. This helps throughput but increases time-to-first-byte for interactive streams unless the proxy flush policy is tuned.
- TCP Nagle interactions: with TCP_NODELAY off, coalescing occurred in TCP stack but at the cost of head-of-line aggregation delaying first bytes. With TCP_NODELAY on, we reduced latency but increased packets and TLS overhead.

Practical mitigations we tested (and short verdicts):
- Adaptive chunking: emit small chunks immediately up to a threshold, then pause and wait for socket writability; this kept first-byte latency low while avoiding kernel queue bloat. Verdict: effective, moderate code complexity.
- Batch-and-flush with a short timer (3–5ms): coalesces bursts but bounds first-byte latency. Verdict: good compromise for most customers.
- TLS-level record bundling: ensure the TLS library can coalesce pending records before writing. On our stack this required changes in how the runtime calls SSL_write. Verdict: helpful but brittle across library versions.
- Tune Envoy flush and buffer filters: reduce default flush interval for streaming routes (from 100ms -> 10ms) and set reduce buffer ceiling. Verdict: helps interactive use-cases but increases CPU on proxy side; needs per-route config.
- Increase HTTP/2 initial window and MAX_FRAME_SIZE for trusted internal traffic. Verdict: good for throughput, but should be gated by policy for cross-tenant/public traffic.

Simple adaptive algorithm sketch (runtime change):
- Goal: keep first-byte latency under threshold T1 (e.g., 20ms) while avoiding >B bytes pending in kernel buffers.
- On token ready:
  1) If time since last emit > T_idle -> emit immediately (fast path).
  2) Else append to small in-memory buffer; if buffer >= B_emit (e.g., 1KB) or timer t_emit (3ms) expires -> flush.
  3) Before flush, check socket writable via poll/select or SO_SNDBUF usage; if kernel buffer > high_water -> defer via event loop until writable.
- This avoids busy spinning and large # of syscalls while preserving low first byte latency for idle interactive sessions.

Repro steps (commands we used):
- Baseline gRPC streaming run (go client): ghz --insecure --proto chat.proto --call Chat.Stream --concurrency 200 --n 2000 --streaming ... (adapt to our client impl).
- HTTP/1.1 streaming with wrk2: wrk -t12 -c200 -d60s --latency --script small-chunks.lua http://server/stream
- Capture: sudo tcpdump -w run.pcap port 443 and then analyze with tshark: tshark -r run.pcap -Y tcp.analysis.retransmission -q -z conv,tcp
- eBPF syscall counts: sudo /usr/share/bcc/tools/syscount.py -p <pid>
- Perf: sudo perf record -F 99 -p <server_pid> -g -- sleep 60; sudo perf report

Open questions / next experiments:
- Quantify energy/cost delta: given AES-GCM cost scaling with small writes, what is per-1k-token CPU cost and how does that map to real cost on Dedicated instances? (follow-up perf runs across instance types)
- How do mobile clients (high RTT, variable bandwidth) change the sweet spot for chunk sizes? We need client-side pacing integration tests.
- Test with HTTP/2 over QUIC (if/when available) — QUIC's packetization and 0-RTT semantics might change the calculus for small writes.
- Evaluate kernel bypass (e.g., io_uring + TLS-offload) to reduce syscall overhead for small writes.

Recommendations (short):
1) Implement adaptive chunking (algorithm above) in the runtime branch and expose two knobs: interactive_mode (aggressive low-latency flush) and throughput_mode (coalesce more).
2) Add a per-route Envoy config for streaming endpoints with tuned flush/buffer settings; put conservative defaults but allow opt-in per tenant.
3) Document best-practice client behavior (client should expect small early bytes and not aggressively retry or close streams on partial frames).
4) Run stage-wide perf runs on Dedicated hardware to measure cost impact; gating change to disable for low-tier customers where CPU overhead matters.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add microbenchmark harness to measure per-token TLS cost (OpenSSL tracepoints).
- Share these notes with solutions-engineering for customer-facing guidance (how to configure proxies, client SDK knobs).
- File a follow-up engineering ticket to prototype io_uring-based write path for the hot path.

Appendix (short):
- Observed symptom patterns: heavy p99 tails tied to kernel send buffer saturation; increased context switches correlate with jittered latency; proxies often hide the problem by coalescing which can mask interactive regressions until real users hit p99.
- Short anecdote: during one run, we saw a single overloaded Envoy worker accumulate 200 small frames and then flush them together causing a 150ms spike for ~1% of streams — this matches our suspicion that proxy flush thresholds are a major lever.

End of notes — this is intentionally informal. Will formalize into an RFC once we have the adaptive-chunking prototype results.
